title: Waynedale's backcourt of Audrey Troyer, Kylie Geiser utilize one basic skill well - The jab step - NewsBreak
text:
By James Simpson II ,
19 hours ago APPLE CREEK — When it comes to the basics of basketball, we all know that familiar word: Fundamentals.
Skills that fall in the line of basketball fundamentals can be a chest pass, bounce pass, overhead pass, pivoting, dribbling with your head up with both the left and right hand, boxing out for rebounds, shooting right-handed and left-handed layups, and getting in a textbook defensive stance.
However, one basic skill that might be underused on the girls high school basketball scene these days is the jab step. That's right — that simple half-step an offensive player with the basketball makes off their non-pivot foot to force a defender to react to their movement.
Some might even call it a lost fundamental tool on the preps level.
More: League races tight in Wayne/Holmes County girls basketball rankings
Waynedale's starting backcourt of senior Kylie Geiser and junior Audrey Troyer don't take utilizing a jab step for granted at all. In fact, they each make it an intentional habit to make great use of the jab step on the court.
As Waynedale's two primary ball handlers for the 14-6 Golden Bears, Troyer and Geiser also often play off the ball. When one of them pops out on the perimeter to receive it, the work begins. It's first getting into a triple-threat position that can setup the many offensive options available.
"We just try and read the defense, use our moves and try to get around our defender," Geiser said of the triple-threat stance. "It gives us a better read if we have a shot, drive or pass."
"I just think it's good to keep it away from the defender, so they can't get steals or tip the ball," Troyer said.
Then here comes the good ol' jab step.
Troyer says she's always used the jab step in all her years playing basketball, while Geiser mentions she's been taught the fundamental skill since she was young.
"My Dad and brother, Zach, taught us at a really young age and I learned it at all the youth camps when I was young," she said. "Being in that triple-threat."
Geiser's father and Waynedale girls basketball head coach, Rick Geiser, says the jab step is something that he's constantly taught all the way down to the youth levels.
"We use it a lot in our youth camps. All the way down to the third grade. We talk about a pro pivot," he said.
The word "pro pivot" is another term used for jab step. Coach Geiser got into full detail of the appropriate use of it.
"When we say 'pro pivot', we're stepping with our lead foot right at the defender to create space," he explained. "Then, when you step back, now you have your jab to play off of. You've created space now and if they react, now you can go. If they don't react, now you can shoot it."
"It's kind of the first move to get them off balance," said Kylie, explaining the benefits of using a jab step. "It's easier then dribbling right away. If you can do a move without even dribbling and get by them, then that's way easier in getting to the rim."
"I think when I jab, then drive, I'm looking for open teammates," Troyer added.
Much of what Waynedale likes to do offensively stems from the play of their backcourt, which involves Geiser (7.7 PPG, 4.8 RPG, 3.0 APG, 2.0 SPG) and Troyer (9.3 PPG, 2.7 APG, 2.5 SPG) employing a jab step that sets up their outside shooting game (both have made 28 3-pointers through 20 games), helps them get into the paint, draw fouls and create opportunities for teammates.
"It benefits them a lot because they both handle it well," Rick said. "They can get the defense in an reactionary mode, then their handles are good enough to beat defenses left and right. They've become really skilled at it."
When it comes to the jab step being used on the high school level, Rick believes sometimes players miss chances to effectively utilize it because they're moving too fast and just take off dribbling when the ball comes their way instead of being more patient.
"A part of the learning process is that kids like to dribble quickly and they give up opportunities because they dribble too quickly," Rick said. "If they play with pace at the right times, then they are so much harder to guard. It's not a natural thing, but I think the more experience they are, the slower they play and the better pace they play with."
That right amount of pace Rick talks about is well-suited in Kylie and Troyer's game, and it shows when they receive the ball. They immediately get into a triple-threat stance and survey the defense and their defender, all while looking to attack with their jab step.
Never rushed. Never in a hurry.
So, do you like to use your jab step to create space or to setup a drive and jump shot?
"Whatever my defender likes to give me," Troyer said, short and sweet.
"Sometimes both of them," said Kylie. "If I don't know how they're guarding, I jab a few times. If I see that they bite on it, I can drive. If they don't, then I know I can just shoot it."
"We preach a lot about being in attack mode and making the right play," Rick said. "When they attack, I'm proud of both of them because they've geared their games to setting up their teammates, as well as when it's time to get a bucket. They're unselfish kids. We're pretty fortunate to have two guards with either being interchangeable. When we need to run something for one, the other can run the point. Vice versa. They give us a lot of flexibility in what we wanna do."
A basic usage of a jab step and they're off. That's all it takes.
